en: The ninety-fourth fascicle of the *Śīlun’s Collected Explanations of the Treatise*, Great Section Three:
Explaining "With Contact as Condition," etc. First, the verses list ten categories; the first is the condition of contact (*sparśa-pratyaya*).
Second, the perfection of view;
third, reality;
fourth, understanding.
Fifth, lack of delight;
sixth, knowledge of the stability of phenomena;
seventh, diligence.
Regarding the eight places of birth and so forth, there are two successive expositions.
In the prose commentary, the first explains the general meaning of the condition of contact (*sparśa-pratyaya*).
Since it is directly perceivable that feeling arises conditioned by contact,
why must one falsely speculate that suffering and pleasure are self-made, made by another, or otherwise? Thus,
the two views are fully understood.
If one abandons the views of no-cause and false causes, one attains the name "fulfillment of vision" (*dṛṣṭiparipūri*) among the five causes;
this fulfillment of vision is explained by means of three conditions.
First, it is because one cannot be turned back from the True Dharma and the Vinaya.
Second, they are also said to have attained right view,
because their aspiration for nirvāṇa is pure.
Third, they are also said to have achieved verified clarity regarding the Buddha.
Because wisdom is purified regarding the objects of knowledge,
one is called a "proponent of the True Dharma" according to these three conditions in their respective order;
this constitutes the first form of attendance.
The second and the actual realization, as well as the third,
are sequentially correlated with the first three conditions.
How is it that from this point onward the five causes are explained?
First, the causes for the miserable realms:
namely, the three types of unwholesome karma and the unwholesome roots—
namely, greed, hatred, and delusion.
Regarding the statement that "the five causes of purification refer to the truths and dependent origination," this means that the cognizing wisdom itself is the cause of purification.
This is the third section: the gateway to understanding reality.
The Master Jinghe’s second [section] is further [treated as] the third,
the gate of the true understanding;
now, we simply do not rely upon it.
The Master Da said:

"If one asks why consciousness (*vijñāna*) and name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*) are not mentioned within the section on the 'Gate of Actual Objects,' the answer is that they are included within what has already been explained."
Regarding those who have become weary of and severed the realm of existence, and are free from desire for it: the absence of desire is the realm of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*).
That which consists of the sets of names (*nāmakāya*), phrases (*padakāya*), and phonemes (*vyañjanakāya*) is called the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
First, because it flows from the most pure dharma-dhātu,
it is also called the dharma-dhātu by way of its cause.
Second, by relying on this cultivation, one is able to realize the dharma-dhātu.
From the perspective of the fruit, it is also called the *dharmadhātu*.
Furthermore, the three modes of expression regarding the *dharmadhātu* are also called the *dharmadhātu*.
From the phrase "by such distinctions as these" onwards...
This explains the names and meanings of the distinctions among conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*).
Fourth is the explanation of the gates of understanding.
Master Jǐng says:
Regarding "there being a formal declaration through various methods" up to "not having even a single doubt":
that which has an intended purpose is called "having various methods. As for "one who does not have a formal declaration through various methods": [it refers to one who lacks such an intention].
Regarding the declaration that "my births are exhausted" and so forth, without any further additions—
how does one know and see when this is the definitive knowledge and discernment?

Regarding the passage "His births have been exhausted," the answer provides a formal declaration (vyākaraṇa), stating: "Because the conditions for birth have been exhausted, his births have been exhausted.
Furthermore, regarding the subsequent section:
This explains the sixth specific exposition:
namely, that which specifically expositions how there is birth conditioned by those very causes and conditions.
Furthermore, he further prophesied that the causal conditions for those births are the various types of grasping (*upādāna*),
and that conditioned by grasping there is existence (*bhava*).
Furthermore, he further prophesied that because one knows these characteristics of grasping as they truly are and sees them as they truly are, grasping will no longer exist.
This is a separate record concerning the abandonment of grasping (*upādāna*).
Having already explained the fifth record on patience (*kṣānti*),
one now proceeds to explain the fourth record on the distinction of abandonment.
All causes and conditions for craving are completely exhausted.
This definitive exposition of abandonment is a specific exposition;
it specifically records the severance of craving.

Therefore, it should be understood that this summary declaration consists briefly of three aspects: first, the initial summary, which is the statement that "I have no fetters whatsoever spoken of by the Buddha";
second, the summary that all evil and unwholesome dharmas do not leak into the mind.
Third, he is personally free from all pride.
Master Da says: "Regarding those who possess the distinct categories of prophetic declarations (vyākaraṇa):"
Regarding such matters as the intention for another time,
I now have not a single doubt; it is not that I attained freedom from doubt merely by hearing [the teaching].
Therefore, it is said that there is a different perspective (*paryāya*).

Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "In the case of those who have already received a prediction," since the prediction is made based on knowledge of the causes, this effectively bypasses the explanation of the sixth [point], which concerns the existence of the causes and conditions for that prediction.
In the previous *jñānapratijñā* (prediction by wisdom), it was stated, "Because the conditions for birth are exhausted.
The "conditions for birth" refers to the members of dependent origination (*bhavāṅga*).
Here, however, it is called the "causal condition for the category of the member of birth."
That which is called "dependent origination" (pratītyasamutpāda) refers to the existence-factor (bhavāṅga).
Furthermore, it records those who grasp at the causal conditions for that birth;
furthermore, it investigates the dependent origination belonging to the category of the existence-factor.
This refers to the limb of grasping (*upādāna*).
Since this is the causal condition (*pratyaya*) of the causal condition school,
it is called "the causal condition of causal conditions."
The preceding section clarifies the contemplation of origination and activity (*utpāda-kriyā-bhāga*).
Furthermore, from the passage "Moreover, having distinguished these various marks of grasping" onwards, it clarifies the contemplation of cessation and extinction (*nivṛtti-bhāga*).
Regarding the "General Summary" (*saṃgraha-viniścaya*):
this refers back to the fifth section, the General Summary,
which restates the text concerning the summary of wisdom (*jñāna-viniścaya*).
Regarding the "determination through abandonment":
this further explains the fourth [section], determination through abandonment;
the fifth [section] explains the lack of delight.
First, there is a general heading listing what is liked and what is not liked;
subsequently, there is an explanation through question and answer.
The sixth [section] explains the knowledge of the persistence of phenomena (*dharma-sthiti-jñāna*) and the knowledge of nirvāṇa (*nirvāṇa-jñāna*).
This is the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthiti-jñāna) prior to the path of vision;
it contemplates the four truths and differs from the Lesser Treatises.
Regarding the "four perfections," they shall be explained below.
This concludes the seventh section: the gateway of diligence.
First, one distinguishes that the six perfections of contemplation can give rise to diligence;
subsequently, it is clarified that [the teaching] is called "well-expounded" by virtue of four characteristics.
Within the former:
First, there is a general enumeration and inquiry;
second, there is a detailed explanation.
Within this, there are two parts.
First, the characteristics of the six kinds of perfection are explained;
subsequently, it is clarified that those who are wise and discerning abide in diligent application.
Within this, there are further two [sections].
First, the practice of diligence is distinguished;
second, diligence and laziness are contrasted to distinguish their respective gains and losses.
This is done within the context of clarifying the benefits of diligence.
First, the two benefits were collectively presented above.
From the passage beginning "This diligence...
onwards, the second section provides an explanation according to specific difficulties, which is divided into three chapters.
The sequential explanation follows.
The first two points are understandable.
Regarding the analysis of the meaning of "simultaneity" (*sahabhū*):
First the question is posed, followed by the answer.
Within the answer, there are two parts:
first, the primary meaning.
Second is the meaning for others.
Within this, there are four propositions;
the fourth proposition follows continuously and without interruption upon the preceding three propositions.
Therefore, it is said that they are "greatly expanded.
Eighth, the explanation of the place of birth can be understood according to the text.
The ninth is the section on resolving doubt (*saṃśaya-vinodana*).
This refers to the first "furthermore" (*punar-apara*) mentioned by the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the verse.
Master Da and others say:
The many learned noble disciples are still ordinary beings;
although they are worldlings, they are so.
They are called "noble disciples" (ārya-śrāvaka) because they study the noble Dharma;
if the two characters "widely learned" (bahuśruta) were removed, they would be true noble ones (ārya).
This text serves as proof of this.
The tenth is the section on the resolution of suffering and affliction.
This refers to what follows after the phrase "such as these" (*ity-ādi*).
As for the statement, "Suppose there is one... up to the third person," it means: suppose there is a certain individual, and so forth, up to the third person.
This passage clarifies that while practitioners still perform the karma of accumulating provisions (*sambhāra-karman*),
they perform only the karma of fulfillment (*paripūri-karman*).
This concludes the fourth major section.
Regarding the explanation of "the cessation of existence" and so forth:
first, the verse enumerates six categories. The first is the cessation of existence (*bhavanirodha*).
Second, śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas;
third, subsequent knowledge;
fourth, saṃsāra.
Five: coming and going; six:
the Buddha’s forward and reverse [order].
In the prose commentary, the first explains the gate of existence and cessation.
Master Jing said:

"All those who have attained the stage of 'seeing the traces' (darśanamārga) have simultaneously realized both body and wisdom at the point where the afflictions of seeing (dṛṣṭi-heya-kleśa) are extinguished;

however, regarding the point where the afflictions of cultivation (bhāvanā-heya-kleśa) have not yet been extinguished, although they perceive cessation through discernment (pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha), their bodies have not yet realized it."
Because it has not yet been severed,
it is like that thirsty person who gazes toward a well and sees water,
together with the water-vessel provided for them.
The method for knowing how to proceed toward cessation is called the "watering vessel.
The Master Da says:

although the noble ones who have attained the path have already realized with the eye of wisdom the unconditioned state where the afflictions to be abandoned by the path are exhausted, [they must still apply this method].
They have also attained the skillful means for practicing the path;
however, they have not yet severed the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation,
nor have they realized the unconditioned.
Therefore, it is said that "one has not yet attained [it].
The allegorical text states:
"The fleshly eye is a metaphor for the Path of Seeing."
The pure water is a metaphor for the unconditioned (asaṃskṛta) that is realized;
the water vessel is a metaphor for the skillful means (upāya) of the path that can cultivate it.
Some explain that "existence" (bhava) here refers to the three realms of existence (tribhava).
When the three realms of existence (*tribhava*) are extinguished, one realizes *nirvāṇa*;
therefore, *nirvāṇa* is called the "extinction of existence.
This is intended to show that those who have attained the three fruits do not rely on external conditions, but realize *nirvāṇa* through their own contemplation.
Yet they have not yet realized it,
like a thirsty person who sees water but does not drink.
This is the second interpretation of śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas.
Master Jing said:
"Furthermore, there are two kinds: first, those produced by craving; second, those produced by karma... up to 'the six sense bases accompanied by the realm of ignorance.
According to the Tripitaka Master, it is as follows:"
These eight factors are produced by craving. Why is this so?
Because craving (*tṛṣṇā*) and grasping (*upādāna*) are both of the nature of greed.
It can be understood that [the link] named craving (tṛṣṇā) is produced by craving;
that karma moistened by craving is called existence (bhava),
which is likewise produced by craving.
From these three branches, two fruits arise.
Tracing back from craving, one sees that which is produced by craving;
furthermore, one views feeling as the basis for craving.
Contact is the basis for feeling;
the six sense bases are the basis for contact.
Therefore, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling further give rise to craving as their fruit, which is called "craving."
This is called "that which is produced.
Because the seeds of ignorance depend upon the six sense bases,
they are called the "six sense bases followed by the realm of ignorance."

Therefore it is said: "If there are sensations produced by contact associated with ignorance, or if there are the six sense bases accompanied by contact associated with ignorance and the element of ignorance;
as for that which is performed by karma, up to not knowing things as they truly are."
Not knowing things as they truly are is ignorance (*avidyā*).
Among the preceding four factors, volitional activity (*saṃskāra*) constitutes the essence of karma;
from this mental karma arise bodily and vocal karma.
Since consciousness and name-and-form are the fruits of karma,
they are said to be "produced by karma.
Since ignorance is the cause of karma, [it is said to be "produced by the cause"].
This is called "the activity of karma.
As stated below in the *Dharmasthitijñāna*,
it clarifies that the preceding [state] does not realize the subsequent path in this manner.
The preceding knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthiti-jñāna) cannot even comprehend dependently arisen phenomena;
how much less can it fully know them as the clear realization of the truths (satyābhisamaya) attained through the path of seeing (darśana-mārga)?
Although the path of seeing abandons the afflictions of wrong views, it does not do so in the manner of the path of cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga).
Therefore, they have not yet attained full and complete knowledge.
Although they have exhausted the afflictions through the cultivation of the path, they are not yet equal to those beyond training (aśaikṣa);
hence it is said that they have not yet been able to transcend.
The Master Da also said:
"Because it gives rise to the other within this,
and because it arises from the other."
Both clarify that which is produced by craving (*tṛṣṇā*):
the link of craving accompanied by grasping (*upādāna*) is that which can produce others.
Therefore, it is called "that which is produced.
From the passage beginning with "if ignorance," it clarifies that [phenomena] arise from others.
Therefore, it is called "that which is produced.
Question: Why is birth, old age, and death not mentioned among those things that can produce others?
Answer: In this context, what is discussed is the activity of the cause.
Since that which is produced necessarily gives rise to a resulting fruit,
one speaks only of the cause and not the fruit.
Within the activity performed by karma, there exists only the capacity to produce another.
Therefore, it is called "that which is performed.
Third is the interpretation of the wisdom of reception (*pratītyajñāna*).
Master Jing and others say:
The forty-four knowledges of reception and the forty-four knowledges of wisdom differ from the Lesser Treatises, which explain only the forty-four knowledges.
It should be understood that herein the four truths are established within the eleven factors.
Based on each of these factors as a truth, forty-four matters are established;
these are the forty-four matters of the truths.
Regarding the statement here that "at the end, old age and death are excluded as being only the fruit;

at the beginning, ignorance is included as being only the cause," this is based on a preliminary and partial view of cause and effect, wherein ignorance is taken to have no prior cause and old age and death are taken to have no subsequent fruit.
If one relies on the twelve links of cyclic existence, ignorance has a cause, which is old age and death;
and old age and death have a fruit, which is ignorance.
This is called the beginningless wheel of existence.
Because ignorance exists only within the [other] three truths and lacks the nature of the origin (samudaya), it is not observed therein;
therefore, there are only forty-four knowledges.
This is due to the distinctions in the thorough knowledge (parijñā) across the three periods of time.
This is the contemplation of causes:
past factors already arisen that condition aging and death,
and future factors yet to arise that will condition aging and death.
The present life consists of old age and death conditioned by the causes of this birth.
This statement refers to the aforementioned definitive and pervasive knowledge of distinctions;
it is an investigation based on careful examination.
In the past, there was no old age, death, and so forth that did not arise through conditions.
Furthermore, there are three types of knowledge which, when added to the previous ones, make six.

This is because the knowledge that apprehends [the nature of things]—which is subsumed under the knowledge of the stability of phenomena (dharma-sthiti-jñāna)—possesses distinctions regarding the characteristic of impermanence.
Observing the three periods of time as a whole,
one sees that old age and death arise from birth;
all are impermanent.
Thus, seven knowledges are established.
In this manner, up to the contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), there are likewise seven knowledges;
therefore, there are seventy-seven knowledges in total.

Thus, one who sequentially contemplates all aspects of the truths and subsequently enters the clear realization of the truths (satyābhisamaya) must clearly understand that these practices were performed prior to the path of vision (darśanamārga).
The fourth [section] explains the process of transmigration (*pravṛtti*). Master Jing says:
"First, regarding the increase of causes..."
The first seven are the causes of attraction;
the second is because the fruit arises;
the third is the cause of production.
Regarding the third [category], the accumulation through augmentation:
when the two causes that produce [results] accumulate toward their respective fruits, they are termed "fruits.
This accumulation through augmentation—such as all these [factors] subsumed into one—is collectively designated as "all phenomena," whether they are augmenting, arising, or accumulating.
The three preceding characteristics combined constitute its forward evolution (*pravṛtti*).
That which depends on the cessation of cause and effect, up to its final disappearance,
is its reversal (*nivṛtti*).
The seven increases mentioned previously are reversed and termed "decrease.
The three causes for arising mentioned previously are reversed and termed "cessation.
The two fruits of accumulation mentioned previously are reversed and termed "disappearance."
The two principles of saṃsāra and cessation do not contradict the characteristics of phenomena (dharmalakṣaṇa);
therefore, it is said that such distinctions in underlying intention do not contravene the nature of reality (dharmatā).
Furthermore, there is another meaning regarding the distinctions of time in terms of the beginning, middle, and end:
The cause of past transmigration is termed "augmentation" (samāropa);
its cessation is termed "extinction" (nirodha).
Future transmigration is termed the "arising of the fruit" (phalotpāda).
In the section on cessation, it is called "diminution";
in the present, it is called the "fruit.
"Accumulation" and "increase" are the opposites of these, and are thus termed "submergence."
Regarding the phrase "due to the distinctions of the desire, form, and formless realms," etc.:
in the desire realm, the process of transmigration and cessation is termed "increase" or "decrease";
in the form realm, it is termed "arising" or "ceasing."
Regarding the statement that "the formless [aggregates] are either arising or ceasing," Master Tai says: first,
there is increase by way of a cause, namely the link of ignorance (*avidyā*).
The augmentation of the two results refers to the members of birth, aging, and death.
The augmentation of the three causes refers to the remaining seven members.
Master Da says:
Regarding "whether increasing, arising, or accumulating," these are all spoken of collectively in one place with reference to the twelve links;
therefore, it says "whether increasing, etc."
As for "cessation," it refers to the cessation of ignorance within the section on cessation; therefore,
it is called "cessation."
If it is "extinguished" (nirodha),
it is called extinguished because of the cessation of formative forces (saṃskāra).
If it is "submerged" (nimagna),...
It is called "passing away" because birth, old age, and death have been exhausted.
Fifth is the explanation of coming and going.
Master Jing says:
Regarding the defilement of karma and craving:
because it is produced by volition associated with craving,
it is called the defilement of karma and craving.
Second, the defilement of false views refers to the various views;
it should be understood that from this point downward [the text] addresses this.
To distinguish their various names:
from "one in training who has seen the path" up to "one who does not delight in future existence," this is one interpretation.
Discriminative views have already been severed and extinguished;
there remains only innate false view,
which is severed for the most part.
Therefore, it is said that there are only the latencies (*vāsanā*).
According to the second interpretation, the views of discrimination (*vikalpa-dṛṣṭi*) are called "entanglements" (*paryavasthāna*);
all of these have been completely severed.
The innate view arises from the cause of conceptual discrimination;
these are collectively termed "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*).
Therefore, it is said that there are only the habitual tendencies of the conceit of self (*asmimāna*) and so forth.
Regarding the defilements of karma and craving that lead to the gathering of future existence:
these are precisely the conceptualization of self-love (*ātmasneha*).
For those who practice the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), this is abandoned through the abandonment of the conceptual view of self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).
This craving ultimately does not function;
however, its seeds remain unsevered and persist as defilement,
which can be understood by those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*).
The Master Da says:
"There are no entanglements" has three different explanations.
One states that there are none arising from conceptual discrimination.
Therefore, it is said that there are no *paryavasthānas* (active outbursts).
Question: If that is so, under which category are those that arise spontaneously (*sahaja*) and effortlessly (*svarasena*) subsumed?
Answer: They are included within the *anuśayas* (latent tendencies).
The second explanation states:
Since even those [afflictions] that are co-emergent (*sahaja*) for the most part do not arise,
it is said that there are no entanglements (*paryavasthāna*).
The third explanation says:
because there is no entanglement of the conceit of self (*asmimāna*) arising from conceptual discrimination. Why is this?
Since the view of self, which serves as its basis, has already been abandoned,
this conceit of "I" (asmimāna) will never again manifest.
However, the explanation in the Tripiṭaka states:
Regarding the various envelopments (*paryavasthāna*) to be abandoned through the cultivation of the path (*bhāvanā-heya*), there is absolutely none mentioned in the treatise;
nor is there any mention of the envelopment or latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*) that arises from conceptual discrimination.
Because it was previously abandoned during the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*),
that which defiles the mind is, according to one interpretation,
the latent tendency (*anuśaya*) of the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*).
One [interpretation] says it refers to the co-emergent afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*) and so forth;
another says it refers to the manifest cravings (*tṛṣṇā*) and so forth.
Thus some masters explain it.
Question: Since there are still those in training who have not yet severed the innate views (*sahaja-dṛṣṭi*),
the Master cannot state that there is only the habitual tendency (*vāsanā*) which serves as the basis for the conceit "I am" (*asmimāna*),
because the term "only" is used in the sense of a definitive restriction.
If it is said that there are manifest activities due to habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), may it also be said that there are manifest activities while being merely habitual tendencies?
Answer: Here, in this fifth section, the intent is to demonstrate that there is no difference between the Great and Small Tripitakas.
Only those lesser sages of later generations take me literally;
if they cling to their own views,
they will dissect my true words.
Consequently, many obstacles arose.
Therefore, the Master of the Treatise, in order to reveal that the Buddha’s intention converges upon a single path,
has composed the *Vastusaṃgrahaṇī*.
However, one cannot on that basis claim that because there are two views in the preceding portion,
there must likewise be two views in the subsequent portion. Why is this?
The intended meaning of this passage is precisely to explain the Tathāgata’s teaching on the characteristics of conformity; therefore,
innate views cannot be described as being entangled with false views.
It speaks only of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).
Because they are subtle, they are not included within these categories; those two views belong to the conceit of self (*asmimāna*).
Master Tai said:
Because those in the three stages of training do not give rise to conceptual views,
false views have already been severed.
The sixth [stage] understands the Buddha’s forward and reverse progression.
Within this, there are three sections: first, the correct interpretation of the Buddha’s forward and reverse order;
second, a general explanation of the members of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*);
and third, the sequential stages of cultivation based on the seven purities.
First, it is explained that the Buddhas of the past and so forth attained bodhi by means of reflecting upon dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Having attained bodhi, they subsequently dwelt in the happiness of the present life (*dṛṣṭadharmasukhavihāra*) by contemplating the forward and reverse sequences of the principle of dependent origination.
Now the Bhagavat is likewise so.
This clarifies that from Śākyamuni Tathāgata back through the seven preceding Buddhas, they all equally contemplated dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) to attain bodhi and so forth. Question:
In the past, there have been immeasurable Buddhas who, by equally contemplating dependent origination, all attained Bodhi.
Why, then, is it said that only the seven Buddhas and so forth [are mentioned]? This is now discussed in order to provide a comprehensive explanation according to our school’s tenet.
Although those [kalpas] are immeasurable, they are said to resemble the seven kalpas of the world as previously described;
that is, seven fires pass in succession, followed by one calamity of water and fire, and so forth.
Therefore, following this analogy, we shall discuss the seven Buddhas for now.
How much more so for the inferior forms of bodhi possessed by others?
Even when the Buddha attained bodhi, it was still like dependent origination; thus, he had not yet realized that which is to be realized, and so forth.
How much less so, then, for the bodhi of the two vehicles?
From this point downward, there is a general explanation of the branches of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "in order to understand as it truly is, up to what was previously stated," this refers to contemplating the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of dependent origination.
The causal condition of dependent origination,
the causal condition of affliction,
and the causal condition of purification.
Purity. These are the five factors.
Furthermore, the general summary of the meaning of this dependent origination is as follows: "Regarding the category of the revolving [existence], there are various sufferings that have causes."
This refers precisely to the causes and conditions for transmigration.

Furthermore, regarding "those dharmas that have causes and are untainted according to the category of reversal," this refers to the wisdom that realizes and abandons all dharmas within the contemplation of the aspect of the cessation of dependent origination.
Furthermore, regarding the nature of those outflows as being based upon the various feelings produced by contact with ignorance:
the feelings produced by contact with ignorance serve as the basis for craving and grasping.
Furthermore, regarding those phenomena that have causes but possess only a basis and an object-condition:
for an Arhat, because they have severed the afflictions, the phenomena that have causes and conditions consist merely of six bases and six objects.
Third, the explanation of the seven purifications (*saptaviśuddhi*).
Those who wish to attain unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*) nirvāṇa by gradually cultivating and accumulating the seven purifications should cultivate the seven purifications of the mind.
The phenomena of birth and death are established in dependence upon causes and conditions;
this is called "conditioned activity.
Nirvana is not so.
It is called "non-creation.
Among the seven purifications, these are the first two: purification of ethical discipline and purification of mind.
Prior to the Path of Seeing:
the third [moment] sees the defiled;
the fourth crosses over doubt regarding the pure.
The fifth and sixth [moments] are in the path of seeing; [the seventh through ninth] are in the path of cultivation.
The seventh is on the path of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣamārga*).
First, purity of morality (*śīlaviśuddhi*) is the prātimokṣa precepts;
purity of mind (*cittaviśuddhi*) is the attainment of the four dhyānas.
Third is the purification of views,
which is the right view of a trainee (śaikṣa) consisting in the clear realization of the truths.
Fourth is the transcendence of doubt.
Doubt regarding the Three Jewels is ultimately severed;

this is precisely the four kinds of indestructible confidence (*aveccappasāda*). Then follows the purification of knowledge and vision regarding what is the path and what is not the path (*maggāmagga-ñāṇadassana-visuddhi*).
One immediately understands that the path preceded by right view is the true path;
by means of this, one can sever the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation.
This is the sixth clear knowledge: the purity of vision regarding the path.
Having attained skillfulness regarding what is the path and what is not the path, one leaves the non-path behind and travels upon the true path. This is the seventh stage:

however, it is solely due to the person who performed these actions that they pass away from those upper realms and fall back into the five destinies.
Therefore, it is said that one is born into the five destinies. Master Da says:
"Regarding the three grades discussed within the faculties (*indriya*):"
One creates karma of three grades;
therefore, one is said to be born in the three evil realms. Furthermore, there is another interpretation.
A single karma undergoes retribution across the three evil realms;
the Mahāyāna is likewise so.
This interpretation is the same as that of Master Jing.
Eleventh, the explanation of the great meaning.
Master Jing said:
"The wisdom that contemplates suffering is like one's original feet."
Because it is attained for the first time,
the knowledge of origin (samudaya-jñāna) abandons the origin,
just as a wall or a fence obstructs a thief.
The knowledge of cessation gradually ascends,
like the lower tiers of a platform;
the knowledge of the path is like the upper terrace.
Regarding the statement that "a person who has seen the noble truths" up to "is like a pebble or the Great Snowy Mountains":
their suffering is as slight as a pebble,
while the greater portion [of it] has been severed, like the snow mountains.
The lower metaphor illustrates the abandonment of craving within the three realms.
The craving already abandoned in the formless realm is like a vast lake;
that which remains unabandoned is like two or three drops. The craving already abandoned in the form realm is like a large pond; that which remains unabandoned is like two or three drops.
The craving of the desire realm that has been severed is like the water of the great ocean,
while that which remains unsevered is like two or three drops.
Furthermore, the Great Snowy Mountains are a metaphor for the suffering produced by the severance of pride.
The analogy of the golden mountain represents the suffering produced by craving for the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*);
Mount Sumeru represents the suffering produced by craving for the form realm (*rūpadhātu*);
and the great earth represents the suffering produced by craving for the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
Master Tai said:
"The wisdom of suffering is like a practitioner setting out with the intent to travel;
the wisdom of accumulation is like reaching the walls and enclosures of the Treasure Terrace."
The knowledge of cessation is like descending to the lower tiers of a terrace;
the knowledge of the path is like reaching the ultimate point at the top of a jeweled terrace.
Master Da said:

The "great purpose" refers to the fact that the untainted path (*anāsrava-mārga*) can attain the great purpose of the Four Noble Truths, as well as the great purpose of realizing unsurpassed enlightenment (*anuttara-bodhi*).
Within this context, pride (*māna*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) pertain to all three realms; the same applies to the body, speech, and mind.
Greed, hatred, delusion, and so forth exist only in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The small portion of suffering present within the bodies of the noble ones (*ārya*) is like pebbles;
for the noble ones have already severed all suffering as completely as the Great Snow Mountains.
The mention of "two drops" and so forth is a metaphor for the suffering that has not yet been severed by the noble ones— namely,
the suffering of only seven more births or even a single lifetime.
Therefore it is said:
as for the metaphor of the six kinds of gravel,
the manifold sufferings produced by the three karmas and the three poisons constitute the six.
This illustrates the six [elements]. The lump of clay represents that which has not yet been severed in the noble body, like a small lump of clay;
that which has already been severed is like the great earth and so forth.
This is the twelfth [section], resolving difficulties.
"Understanding" refers to the wisdom of hearing;
"superior understanding" refers to the wisdom of reflection;
and "definitive understanding" refers to the wisdom of cultivation.
The ten kinds of true dharmas refer to the eightfold noble path and the wholesome dharmas associated with the correct knowledge of liberation.
The ten courses of action refer to those consisting of two, three, and so forth.
The second refers to the two: volitional action (*kṛta*) and non-volitional action (*akṛta*).
The three types of karma constitute the third.
Furthermore, there is another interpretation: two kinds of threefold karma—
first, the threefold karma of body and so forth.
The two types of merit and so forth refer to the three kinds of karma.

In the ninety-sixth fascicle, from the preceding analysis of dependent origination, nutriment, the truths, and the elements, the first general verse has listed its six sections to complete the explanation of dependent origination, nutriment, and the truths.
From here below, the second section consists of a half-verse that enumerates three gates in general;
it specifically clarifies the discernment of the elements (*dhātu-vicaya*),
first as the general meaning and so forth.
The second [verse] concerns light and so forth;
the third concerns feeling and so forth.
Below are four distinct verses explaining the first half-verse.
The explanation of the initial general meaning consists of four sections:
first, the general meaning;
second, the specific categories.
Third, the three semblances of transformation;
fourth, the three types of seeking.
[These appear] in the prose section.
First, regarding the general meaning:
Master Jing says that herein,
both the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) as they manifest and the seeds of the eighteen elements are called "abiding in their own nature" (*prakṛtistha*).
The Master Da says:
"Dwelling in the realm of self-nature" refers exclusively to the eighteen realms as they manifest and as latent tendencies (anuśaya) within the indeterminate (avyākṛta).
"Those that increase the realms" refers to those of a wholesome or unwholesome nature.
This is the second explanation, distinguishing their specific categories.
Regarding the "great akṣa cluster," the Tripiṭaka Master states:
"The characteristics of the akṣa are such that it is not the same as the *wushi* (jujube) fruit found here."
First, it is capable of being dyed;
second, oil can be pressed from it.
Every household possesses it, whether in small quantities or in large amounts.
The third [section] explains the semblance transformation as in the text.
The fourth [section] explains among the three types of seeking.
First, regarding the explanation of the holy life (*brahmacarya*) that has been attained:
it is said that these two serve as its basis.
First, there is the absence of delusion and loss of mindfulness regarding what has long been practiced.
Second, what has been spoken for a long time is without falsehood or loss of mindfulness.
To say "thus" is to speak of the gradual cultivation of the three trainings through the predominant power of faith;
this concludes the previously explained realm of ignorance.
From "the six sense bases that are followed" onwards,
it clarifies that the realm of craving is the seed;
furthermore, from "the realm of ignorance" onwards...
The following explains the desire for seeking.
Next, there is one verse that interprets the second [section], "first" and so forth;
it contains seven gates.
First, the inclusion of the thirty-seven factors;
second, views and perceptions; third, wonders.
Fourth, differentiation;
fifth, establishment;
sixth, tranquility.
Regarding the seven types of fools:
in the prose commentary,
the first section explains how the twenty-one realms are subsumed within one another.
First, the three realms and seven realms were enumerated.
Many people explain this by saying that the form realm (rūpadhātu) also includes the desire realm (kāmadhātu).
The textual phrasing does not seem to subsume [the preceding] matter.
One should know that from this point downward,
the second section distinguishes their mutual inclusion.
Furthermore, regarding the craving for form (*rūparāga*) below [the realm of desire],
it specifically explains the first two of the seven [realms] because they are difficult to perceive.
Regarding the statement, "From [attachment] through views and through feeling, up to the pure realm," Master Jing says:
"In the stages of the form realm (rūpadhātu), greed arises by means of views."
From sensation arises craving,
which is called darkness;
as an antidote to that, one contemplates impurity.
One establishes the realm of light;
in order to abandon the practice of the contemplation of impurity, one again contemplates pure forms and establishes the realm of purity.
This is the liberation of purity.
Master Da said:
"It is by means of vision that the realm of luminosity is revealed."
This refers to the third dhyāna and above.
By means of feeling (*vedanā*), the pure realm (*viśuddhadhātu*) is manifested;
that is to say, the form (*rūpa*) and so forth of the fourth dhyāna.
Furthermore, below these seven elements,
one is exhorted to know the seven elements; one should understand that the full comprehension (*parijñā*) of the seven elements is what must be realized.
"This is the first gate.
Regarding 'one should understand the means for attainment,' this is the second gate."
One should understand that which is attained;
this is the third gate.
Regarding that which is for the sake of which one should understand:
This is the fourth gate.
Following these four gates, one sequentially liberates from the first gate.

Thus, all thorough knowledges (*parijñā*) regarding the various elements (*dhātu*) should be understood through four causes and conditions; namely, that there is a contradiction between the remedy and that which is to be remedied, and they are mutually dependent.
This is the first cause.
This is the second cause, because the limited and the immeasurable depend upon one another as conditions.
Existence and non-existence constitute the third cause,
because they are mutually dependent as being superior and non-superior.
This is the fourth cause.
Regarding the statement that light is designated based on darkness as its condition, and purity is designated based on impurity as its condition:
the arising of desire for form is called "darkness."

The first two liberations involve the cultivation of the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*) to counteract craving for form (*rūpa-rāga), and thus the "element of light" (*āloka-dhātu*) is established.
This refers to such [liberations] as "possessing internal form, one perceives external forms," and "not possessing internal form, one perceives external forms," and so forth.
In order to abandon the impure, one again contemplates pure forms; thus, the "pure realm" (*śubhadhātu*) is established, which is precisely the "pure liberation" (*śubhavimokṣa*).
Therefore, it is said that based on the impure as a condition, the pure is designated, and based on the sphere of form (*rūpāyatana*) as a condition, space (*ākāśa*) is designated.
All forms are contemplated as empty;
this is what is meant by "because they are mutually contradictory.
As for the statement, "the antidote is designated in dependence upon that which is to be remedied," etc.:
The first three realms are established based on the first cause.
Next, it is said that the sphere of infinite consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*) is designated because consciousness takes a limited object as its condition;
this establishes the sphere of consciousness based on the second cause.
Next, regarding the statement, "The sphere of nothingness is designated by taking the minor degree of existence as its condition," this establishes the sphere of nothingness based on the third cause.
Following that, the passage beginning with "by the supreme manifestation of all existence" and so forth [is stated].
It is understood that the sixth and seventh realms are established by virtue of the fourth [dhyāna] serving as the causal condition for both the higher and the unsurpassed;
this is the thorough knowledge according to the first method.
The second [section] below explains the thorough knowledge regarding attainment.
Furthermore, there is a meditative absorption called "with effort" (*sābhisaṃskāra*), up to and including the attainment of the absorption of the Peak of Existence (*bhavāgra*);
this is the sixth element.

Because one does not conceptualize any perceptions and because one correctly contemplates the signless realm (*animitta-dhātu*), the cessation of the view of a self-identity (*satkāya-nirodha*)— that is,
the analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) which is the object of the signless samādhi— is called the "realm of cessation" (*nirodha-dhātu*).

Regarding the phrase "by virtue of being signless, one accordingly attains the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*) and the realm of cessation (*nirodhadhātu*)," this text explains that the seventh realm of cessation includes the meditative absorption of cessation as well.
These two types are "attained accordingly by not relying on the concentration of application" (*prayoganiyama*).
First, analytical cessation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*); second, the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
This is because one does not abide in liberation by means of a meditative concentration based on conceptual mental constructions (*saṃjñā-vicāra*).
There is conditioned liberation and unconditioned liberation for one who abides in liberation.
The third section from here below concerns what should be understood regarding that attainment; specifically,
it refers to how these various meditative concentrations reach the point of being designated as the "attainment of the respective realms."
The following clarifies the fourth point, which should be understood as that which is to be attained.

Furthermore, regarding these various realms (*dhātu*), one should know that they enable the sequential attainment of the eight liberations (*aṣṭa-vimokṣa*). Specifically, the first realm enables the sequential attainment of the first and second [liberations].
The first liberation is subsumed within the realm of light.
As for the statement that "the second realm can subsequently attain the third and so forth," the second pure realm subsumes the pure liberation.
As for the remaining five elements, they enable one to successively attain the five liberations:
those comprised within the four formless realms constitute the four formless liberations, and that comprised within the realm of cessation constitutes the liberation of cessation.
The second [section] explains the characteristics of seeing (*darśana-lakṣaṇa*).
There are two successive expositions; in the first exposition, it says: "These two speakers are the practitioner.
This means that the speaker is one and the same as the practitioner.
The practitioner constitutes the second [category].
Furthermore, within the intermediate [category],
there is first the person of dull faculties.
The first is one who single-mindedly believes in all the philosophical tenets taught by others;
the second is not a person of dull faculties,
but rather one who believes only in those views that they themselves accept, regardless of which philosophical tenet they may follow.
One does not believe in the views and tenets devised by others;
this is the third type of person with sharp faculties,
who has no belief in any of them whatsoever.
Within this, there are two parts:
first, the explanation of the practice of wrong views;
second, the explanation of the practice of right views.
Third, it is further said: Moreover,
if one has a firm attachment toward the training rules one has undertaken— so much so that it could even burn them away—
a person with such firm attachment is like a house made of reeds.
Having few wholesome qualities, they are like insects in a house;
stubbornly adhering to false views, they are like a fire that burns down the house and its roots of virtue—
namely, this *pudgala* who has even fallen away from meritorious and wholesome dharmas.
The Tripitaka Master explains that the wisdoms of hearing,
reflection, and cultivation are called "firm grasping," as they are able to counteract the preceding fires.
There is the person who, like one previously holding a torch, possesses a firm attachment to what has not been heard, reflected upon, or cultivated;
such a person falls away from their meritorious qualities.
One should know that those who are the opposite of this possess renunciation and so forth.
Contrary to those who previously lacked hearing, reflection, and cultivation,
one should know that they have emerged from false attachments;
that is, they perceive non-anger, non-harmfulness, and so forth.
The Tripitaka Master says:
One should state that, being the opposite of this, one should know how to emerge from it as appropriate.
This is because the absence of ill will and harm emerges from the factors that are the opposites of those previously mentioned.
The preceding three sections have completed the explanation of the characteristics of views.
From here on, the third section explains that the Buddha possesses two wonders:
first, the manifestation of non-self.
Furthermore, the karma of good and evil does not cease.
There are two types of sentient beings:
the first is the householder.
Second is the renunciant.
Regarding householders, the initial application of effort undertaken in pursuit of wealth and treasures is called the "element of initiation," which refers to seeking small amounts of material goods.
The following clarifies the seeking of great wealth and treasures:
that is, when these various elements move from their own location to another location without having been discarded,
prior to the time of separation from the household.
Regarding those who have already been expelled:
when separated from their wives and children,
they belong to both places simultaneously.
First, the state not yet attained;
second, the state already attained.
Sentient beings who have gone forth first delight in renunciation because their seeking is slight.
The subsequent section on "Great Diligence" and so forth is titled "Great Seeking. This is the fourth explanation of the nature of differentiation,
as per the text.
Fifth is the explanation of the formal establishment.
Based on four causes and conditions, three types of realms—the three realms and two realms of transcendence—are established.
As for the four causes:
First, regarding the three types of "non-emergence and emergence" and so forth:
first, the three realms such as the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) and so on.
Second, the realm of the cessation of form and formlessness;
third, the realm of abandonment, cessation, and dispassion.
Second, the realm of renunciation.
There are five kinds and six kinds.
Among these, the desire realm is established with sensual craving as its condition;
the first dhyāna of the form realm is established as the departure from this realm.
Regarding the establishment of the upper three dhyānas by way of the meaning of renunciation from vitarka, joy, and bliss,
the text is incomplete;
it should fully state that the two dhyānas are established by way of renouncing vitarka and vicāra.
The three dhyānas are established because of renunciation through joy;
the fourth dhyāna is established because of renunciation through bliss.
The sphere of infinite space is established by means of renunciation through the perception of the diversity of forms and their resistance.
The perception of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*) is the perception of blue, yellow, and so forth.
The perception of resistance (*pratigha-saṃjñā*) is the perception of long, short, and so forth.
Combining these two preceding [perceptions] constitutes the perception of manifold natures (*nānātva-saṃjñā*).
This differs from the explanation in the Hinayana:
that which arises from form is the perception associated with visual consciousness.
"Those who respond" refers to the perception associated with the four consciousnesses.
"Various natures" refers to...
It is the category of perception associated with the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

Because the three higher [formless attainments] are established on the basis of the meaning of transcendence through the perceptions of space, consciousness, and nothingness, they constitute the first [category].
As for the [remaining] four, they are so designated because they signify transcendence despite not being external transcendence.
The three realms, beginning with the desire realm,
are established. Furthermore, below the form realm,
it is clarified that the three realms are again established by virtue of the second cause.
Furthermore, it is not the case that within the form realm (rūpadhātu) there is no ultimate [realization] below that;
this clarifies that the three realms are established again by means of the third cause for those who are free from overweening pride (adhimāna).
The following clarifies how the two realms of transcendence (*niḥsaraṇadhātu*) are established based on the fourth cause,
as explained in the eleventh fascicle.
The sixth [section] explains tranquility (*śānti*).
As stated in the text.
Seventh, regarding the explanation of the fool:
first, the characteristics of the foolish and the wise are distinguished.
Following this, there is a detailed analysis according to the meaning.
Within the preceding section, first the characteristics of the foolish are distinguished,
and subsequently the characteristics common to the wise are revealed.
Regarding the preceding section:
first, the two types are presented and enumerated;
subsequently, the two types are explained.
Although he practices correctly, he causes others to suffer;
by practicing wrongly,
he harms the wives and children as well as the wealth and possessions of others.
Although he practices correctly,
he still produces suffering for others;
furthermore, this extends from the formless realm downward.
Following the meaning, this analysis shall distinguish only the four locations of the second characteristic.
First, it clarifies the reason for establishing the sixty-two elements (*dhātu*).
There are thirteen distinctions of superiority.
In the *Dīrgha Āgama*,
the three realms of desire, ill-will, and so forth are established based on defiled perceptions and discursive thoughts.
Based on the purity of vitarka, the three realms of non-desire, non-hatred, and so forth are established.
Furthermore, because the two categories of defilement and purity within these three realms possess the sense of universal pervasion, there are the other four elements and so on.
The four aggregates pertain to all three realms because they encompass both the defiled and the pure; form, however, is not so.
There are three types of "resolving the boundary" (sīmā-vimocana):
namely, the general meaning and so forth, light and so forth, and reception and so forth.
Of these, the first two have already been explained.
Next, the third [section] is explained:
regarding sensation (*vedanā*) and so forth, there are two verses;
the first verse contains nine gates.
First, intrinsic nature;
second, causes and conditions;
third, views.
Fourth, the defilements;
fifth, the person; sixth, the distinctions of transformation.
Seven principles,
eight tranquilities,
and nine observations.
The prose section provides two further explanations.
First, it correlates the nine gates listed in the root verses;
second, it explains them in sequential order.
First, their intrinsic nature,
which consists of the three feelings;
second, their causal conditions.
This refers to the contact of suffering, the contact of pleasure, and the contact of neither-suffering-nor-pleasure.
Second, from "Furthermore, all pleasures" onwards,
explains the faults of painful sensation (*duḥkhā vedanā*).
Regarding the phrase "because it can continue to accord with the two [types of suffering]":
Master Jing says that this is because one abandons [the first type] but does not separate from the suffering of suffering (*duḥkhaduḥkhatā*) and the suffering of change (*vipariṇāmaduḥkhatā*).
"This is the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). Master Da said:
"Following the cessation of this neutral feeling (*upekṣā-vedanā*), either a painful feeling or a pleasant feeling arises in succession."
Because it can give rise to the two feelings of pleasure and pain in succession,
it is said that "it continues further within the two.
Fourth, regarding the passage beginning with "From within the feeling of pleasure, there is the latent tendency of attachment (*rāgānuśaya*)."
This explains defilement.
A question is asked:
"Regarding all feelings such as pleasant feeling (*sukha-vedanā*), as long as all afflictions (*kleśa*) remain uneliminated during their manifest states (*pratyupasthita-avasthā*)."
Since both of these feelings arise as being bound by the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) of all afflictions (*kleśa*),
why is it said only that "in pleasant feeling there is the latent tendency of greed, and in painful feeling there is the latent tendency of hatred," and so forth?
Therefore, the treatise provides a general explanation:
"Regarding all feelings such as pleasure, and so forth...

[it is] for the sake of permanently destroying the latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) and for the mature cultivation of the holy life (*brahmacarya*), and not merely for the purpose of dispelling the causes and conditions of the active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*)."
One cultivates the holy life for the sake of abandoning all latent tendencies (*anuśaya*),
not merely for the sake of abandoning those active outbursts (*paryavasthāna*).
This begins from the person who lacks the power of analytical discernment.
First, the explanation of the enumeration of the bases for grasping; second, the explanation of the distinctions in their transformation, based on the nature and support of those various feelings.
7. Furthermore, from "all suffering sensations of all sentient beings" onwards, the reasoning is explained.
8. Furthermore, from "it should be known that those sensations are briefly of three kinds of tranquility" onwards...
"Understanding tranquility" and "delighting in discourse" constitute the second level of explaining tranquility.
Master Jing said:
"This text clearly proves that subtle vitarka exists during the state of meditative concentration.
The Tripitaka Master [Xuanzang] often says that vitarka and vicāra exist during the preparatory stage (prayoga), but are absent once one has entered concentration."
Therefore, [the presence of] subtle vitarka and vicāra exists only in the preparatory stage (sāmantaka) of concentration,
not in the fundamental dhyāna itself.
This present text states that within the concentration there is subtle vitarka and vicāra.
It does not mention either the root or the preliminary application;
that the Path is universally attainable is logically unobjectionable.
The Master Da said:
"The Tripiṭaka Master’s interpretation of this passage is established according to the provisional (upāya) teachings.
As for what I am discussing:"
This refers to the fundamental meditative absorptions (*mauladhyāna*).
From "Furthermore, by means of seven modes of activity" onwards,
it explains analytical observation (*vipaśyanā*).
Among the seven aspects for contemplating feelings within all feelings,
the second aspect— feeling as cause—
is divided into three types in the commentary.
This refers to the causes and conditions for the present process of saṃsāra and its cessation.
For the future, one should contemplate them separately:
saṃsāra as one and cessation as another.
Thus, seven characteristics are established.
Within the second verse, there are seven gateways.
The first is the arising of sensation.
Second, inferiority;
third, the distinctions among the various characteristics of sensation;
fourth, views and so forth as being supreme.
Fifth, the differentiation of knowledge;
sixth, questioning;
seventh, answering.
In the prose section,
the first part explains the arising of birth;
it begins by opening the chapter and establishing the thesis.
Next, the specific explanations are examined in detail;
therein are two parts.
First, the assembly of sentient beings is elucidated.
Subsequently, this section provides a detailed analysis of the arising of various sensations (*vedanā*).
The text is divided into two parts.
The first part analyzes the arising of various sensations by distinguishing between the householder and the renunciant.
The subsequent section distinguishes [the teaching] by means of external paths and internal dharmas.
Within the preceding middle section, first, it distinguishes the two conditions that give rise to sensation by means of the two assemblies.
Subsequently, the two assemblies are distinguished separately.
First, the householders are explained.
It says: "Furthermore, due to the initial manifestation of defiled desire-thoughts, one experiences the various feelings produced by those conditions."
Regarding the sequence of the first three gates:
first is desire, second is vitarka, and third is contact.
Within the latter three meanings:
First, the power of attachment gives rise to that desire;
second, the power of mental attention gives rise to those discursive thoughts.
Third is the power of the objective sphere.
This immediately gives rise to contact,
which, through defiled attachment and refusal to relinquish it, continues in succession for a long time without attaining tranquility.
This is the differentiation of the gates of ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*).
Furthermore, from "those [afflictions] such as desire" onwards,
they manifest due to three conditions.
The afflictions of that category remain within the practitioner’s body and have not yet been permanently severed;
this is the second distinction of the gate of meaning.
The second clarifies renunciation.
Regarding those who have gone forth but have not yet abandoned craving:
since they originally went forth in order to relinquish desire,
they attain tranquility through the desires that are embraced by the power of their attachment.
Sustained by the power of the objects of mental attention, discursive thought and contact have not yet been stilled.
For this reason, regarding those objects of contact, one has not yet cultivated the antidote to discursive thought nor produced detachment.
Improper attention toward previously experienced objects occurs simultaneously with [other mental states];
contact occurs toward excellent and sublime objects;
and if, regarding discursive thoughts, one perceives their faults and develops weariness as previously described, one attains tranquility.
By means of these causes and conditions, applied thought (*vitarka*) is likewise stilled; this is the first dhyāna, free from desire.
However, only contact (*sparśa*) has not yet been stilled; if one encounters an exquisite object, defiled contact arises.
One has not yet abandoned the desire for the second dhyāna and those above it.
If one has already become free from craving for all sensual desires,
there is total tranquility;
this is the distinction of the single gateway.
This refers to those who have already abandoned the desires of the second dhyāna and above.
Furthermore, there is another class mentioned below,
namely those who have not yet abandoned their greed.
Because greed regarding the various desires has not been abandoned,
and because defiled contact with discursive thoughts has not been permanently severed,
none of them have attained tranquility.
If one has already abandoned craving for sensual desires and realized the first dhyāna,
yet the desire for those [meditative] states is not yet stilled—
ranging from one who is free from craving for the first dhyāna up to one who is not yet free from craving for the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception.
Second, having already stilled the contact that was not yet stilled,
one transcends the Peak of Existence; all is stilled.
This is called the second gate of differentiation.
Because it was stated in the preceding gate that one leaves the household life out of weariness with desire,
once desire has arisen toward phenomena characterized by attachment, one attains tranquility [in that regard], while the remaining two are not yet tranquilized.

Furthermore, there is another class of persons who have not yet abandoned craving for sensual pleasures; because they have not severed their attachment to these pleasures, they have not attained tranquility in any respect.
This refers to those who, having abandoned craving for sensual pleasures, have already attained the first dhyāna.
This is the same as the preceding [section].
Below, the arising of various feelings (*vedanā*) is distinguished by means of both non-Buddhist and Buddhist teachings.
The preceding [section] distinguished the non-Buddhists.
Next, the internal dharma is explained.
Furthermore, regarding one who abides in the internal dharma until, conditioned by that which has not yet become tranquil, feeling arises:
the four stages of approach are called the path of approach.
Furthermore, seven types of persons may simultaneously be directed toward the state of no-more-learning (aśaikṣa), and are all termed "those proceeding toward the path" (pratipannaka).
According to the second interpretation, the gate of inferiority and equality involves abandoning five factors and cultivating five factors,
as indicated in the *Samāhitābhūmi*.
The Master Da said:
"One who is able to sever the five dharmas—

Furthermore, regarding the inferior, middling, and superior grades of joy, pleasure, and equanimity:
joy is inferior when it pertains to the desire realm,

pleasure in the desire realm and the first dhyāna is inferior,

Master Jing’s commentary states:
Therefore, it is not the case that karma intentionally created which is to be experienced as suffering is invariably obtained;
such karma pertains to both the wholesome and the unwholesome.
Why is it said that one will certainly experience suffering?
Why is it that even for one who abandons [sensation] in the present life and attains parinirvāṇa, this is not necessarily the case?

Because the equanimity that is free from both suffering and pleasure—the equanimity of sensation—is not fixed as leading to parinirvāṇa in the present life, since this equanimity is attained by both ordinary persons and noble ones alike.
These two further points should be explained through analytical response (*vibhajya-vyākaraṇa*). Master Da says:
"Or, one may attain equanimity (*upekṣā*)."

Therefore, regarding karma created through intentional thought, there is the possibility of relinquishing it; even for one who is certain to attain parinirvāṇa in the present life, this is not invariably so.
If someone were to ask: "Do all noble ones (āryas) necessarily attain parinirvāṇa in the present life? [the answer would be as follows].
Now, I shall answer by way of analysis, stating that it is not absolute because it is indeterminate.

Regarding the statement, "Furthermore, all Tathāgatas skillfully avoid the arguments of others," and so forth:
The Master Tai and others say:
"When an outsider asks about the self and so forth,
these are matters for which a definitive answer should not be given."
However, when he posed an indefinite question, asking whether the self (*ātman*) and the body are one or different,
the Tathāgata avoided it by remaining silent.
Second, regarding the distinct meanings of phenomena such as joy, pleasure, and form:
This is a case where one asks an indeterminate question regarding identity or difference concerning a dharma that ought to be definitively declared.
Furthermore, it is an indeterminate question because pleasure (*nandi*) and the afflictions of the four graspings (*catasra upādānāni*) have distinct meanings.
The Tathāgata is able to avoid them all.
